title: US nuclear fusion firm gets New Mexico's green light to use tritium for net facility gain
excerpt: New Mexico has issued its first private fusion tritium license to Pacific Fusion, marking a major regulatory milestone for the startup.
content:
A $1 billion fusion facility under construction in New Mexico has received the state's first-ever radioactive materials license for a private fusion company.

The New Mexico Environment Department (NMED) issued the permit to the American startup Pacific Fusion. It clears the firm to possess and use tritium at its Albuquerque Research and Manufacturing Campus. 

The approval arrives roughly a year after the company selected New Mexico for the project. Site construction kicked off in August, and Pacific Fusion will continue working closely with state regulators as work progresses toward operational readiness.

Engineers at the facility are racing to test a pulsed-power fusion machine by 2030. Their ultimate objective is to reach "net facility energy gain," a milestone no laboratory has ever achieved. This benchmark is considered essential for bringing clean, affordable fusion energy to the power grid.

Measuring fusion efficiency

Most previous laser and magnetic fusion experiments measured success narrowly. Researchers only compared the energy hitting the fuel capsule against the energy released by the fusion reaction.

Pacific Fusion is setting a much higher bar by measuring efficiency across the entire plant. To hit net facility gain, the fusion reaction must generate more energy than the total electrical energy stored in the machine before it fires.

Achieving this requires a different engineering approach. Pacific Fusion's system relies on pulsed-power inertial confinement. It does not use massive laser arrays or magnetic coils like tokamaks. On the contrary, the system discharges intense bursts of electrical current directly into a target. 

The high-current pulse then creates extreme magnetic pressure. This, in turn, rapidly compresses a small fuel capsule to initiate fusion. To keep manufacturing costs manageable, the power systems use modular, standard electrical components made of widely available industrial materials.

Because fusion does not carry the same risks as traditional nuclear fission, NMED regulates it under a framework similar to hospitals and research labs. Under the new permit, the small quantities of tritium used during operations will remain sealed inside a closed system. Any resulting radioactive waste will be shipped out of state for safe disposal at a licensed facility.

Emerging fusion ecosystem

State leaders view the project as a key driver for New Mexico's Energy Transition Act, which mandates a zero-carbon electricity future. Environment Secretary James Kenney said the milestone proves the state has the talent and infrastructure to lead clean energy innovation. He added that the project will create good-paying jobs while safeguarding public health and the environment.

Pacific Fusion's Co-founder and Chief Operating Officer, Carrie von Muench, credited state regulators for moving quickly and responsibly on the first-of-a-kind facility. She noted that New Mexico's scientific expertise and advanced manufacturing base position it to become a central hub for America's emerging fusion ecosystem. This growth will bring long-term investment and economic opportunity to the region.

"We're excited about what this milestone means, not just for Pacific Fusion, but for the jobs, investment and long-term economic opportunity that fusion can bring to New Mexico," concluded Muench.
